description: A page is now chosen from the segments' stored columns and only the winners are built into result rows. That is a cost change and must never be an answer change, so these cases pin the two routes against each other on one corpus: an ordinary bounded page, and the same answer forced onto the route that builds as it goes by an operator no row view can evaluate. Two more cover the exclusions: an ordering by a field a row view is not allowed to see, and a page cut past an OFFSET, which the older trim over built rows never bounded at all. Read their limit honestly. Every one of them checks an ANSWER, and this change is defined not to move answers, so none of them can tell a column-chosen page that has silently stopped happening from one that is working. That was measured, not assumed: disabling the ranking outright leaves one pre-existing case in the whole suite red, and disabling the deferred-predicate exclusion leaves every case green. The mechanisms are pinned in fast_paths/tests.rs, which does go red; what these cases add is that the two routes agree on a real corpus, which no tempdir fixture can say.

cases.name: the_answer_this_suite_measures_against
cases.description: The whole ordered answer, at a limit past its own size so that nothing is shed. Seven functions in this corpus exceed 150 lines, in this order by size, and every case below asks for a prefix of these. It is not a built-path control and no longer claims to be: a page is cut from row views at any limit, so a limit above TOPK_THRESHOLD only means the trim over built rows is not what bounds it. The built-path control is the regex case below.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE lines > 150 ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 1001

cases.name: a_predicate_deferred_to_built_rows_is_answered_the_same
cases.description: A predicate deferred past materialisation, answered correctly. A regular expression is handed to the filter over built rows unconditionally -- compiling it once for a batch beats once per row -- so it is deferred on every segment whatever columns that segment holds. `name` is not the point: a row view holds `name` and could answer an equality or a LIKE on it; what defers this predicate is the operator. What this case pins is the answer, and only the answer. Removing the exclusion that keeps such a segment out of the ranking does NOT change it -- measured, not assumed -- because the name index narrows the candidate set in Stage 1 first, leaving this segment far below the row count at which any ranking arms. That is close to general: a predicate selective enough that ranking ahead of it would move the page is usually selective enough to shrink the segment below the threshold too, which makes this exclusion very hard to observe end to end at all. It is pinned instead by a_predicate_still_to_run_keeps_every_matched_row in fast_paths/tests.rs, which does fail when the exclusion is removed; this case checks the two agree on a real corpus.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE name MATCHES 'stream_names_desc_kind_filtered' ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 1

cases.name: the_running_trim_inside_the_column_ranked_page
cases.description: The ordinary bounded page, cut from the columns end to end. ORDER BY lines is admitted even on the many segments holding no lines column at all, because a view and the row it would build both report that field as absent and rank identically on it -- that admission is what makes the route reachable. The predicate reader once disagreed, refusing an absent field and so leaving the route taken by almost nothing; it now agrees, and a WHERE on a field some segments lack is answered from that absence rather than deferred. The candidate set is every function in the corpus, and every one of them travels as a 48-byte row view: filtered, collapsed, ranked and cut to five, with five result rows built at the end. It used to be per segment and conditional -- a segment had to hold more matching rows than the trim's own threshold before it would rank rather than build, so on the sibling workspace 56 of 298 function-bearing files cleared it and the rest built what they matched. That per-segment route still exists and still narrows the built path where a predicate keeps a query off this one. The answer must be the same five rows in the same order as the whole ordered answer above.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 5

cases.name: an_ordering_the_columns_cannot_rank_still_answers
cases.description: ORDER BY usages is excluded from the column-ranked route by construction, and this case has no other disqualifier -- its one WHERE is answerable from the columns, so nothing is left to run after a row is built -- which makes the ordering field itself the reason. The per-segment usages column is a stale always-zero legacy field and the real workspace count is stamped onto a row only after it is built, so a row view is not allowed to see it at all: it reports the field absent rather than zero. A regression admitting this query to the column route would therefore rank every row equal, leaving the tie-breakers to choose which rows each file contributes before their real counts were known. These five are the most-used symbols in the corpus at 1544 uses each, so the tie-breakers order them among themselves here too; what this case pins is that they are the five, which a ranking blind to usages could only get right by accident.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' ORDER BY usages DESC LIMIT 5

cases.name: the_same_page_when_a_regex_keeps_it_off_the_view_route
cases.description: The built route answering the page an earlier case answers from views, over the same rows. `name MATCHES '^'` matches every name -- the empty pattern anchors at position 0 of any string -- so the row set is untouched and the operator alone changes the route: a regular expression is compiled once for a batch of built rows rather than once per row, so it waits for built rows on every segment and no page can be cut ahead of it. This is the built-path control the LIMIT 1001 case used to be, and the pair is the only cross-route claim writable from the agent side: a golden case cannot list a frozen corpus's page, so 'the two routes return the same rows' is pinned by construction -- the same clauses reach the engine -- plus the rows named here.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE name MATCHES '^' ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 5

cases.name: a_page_past_an_offset_is_still_cut_from_the_columns
cases.description: An OFFSET disarms the trim over built rows -- shedding on rank is unsound while a skip is still to come -- so this shape used to build every matching row. A page cut from views carries LIMIT + OFFSET of them instead, because the skip runs downstream, after a session's uncommitted rows have been merged in, and a dirty row landing ahead of the window shifts which persistent rows fall inside it. These are rows three and four of the whole ordered answer above.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE fql_kind = 'function' WHERE lines > 150 ORDER BY lines DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2

cases.name: a_predicate_some_segments_have_no_column_for_answers_the_same
cases.description: Mixed coverage: 21,983 of this corpus's 32,748 candidate segments carry no `lines` column at all, and one such segment among the candidates used to take the page off row views for every segment that has one. It no longer does. The row those segments would build carries `lines` in neither its struct nor its enrichment map, so the view and the row both resolve it to None and the predicate is decided from the columns — a segment with no column contributes nothing, which is exactly what it contributed before, minus the rows built to find that out. This case pins the answer, which must not move.

cases.name: the_same_mixed_coverage_answer_under_an_order_by
cases.description: The same predicate with an ordering written, so the page is ranked rather than taken in segment order. Same count, because what changed is where the predicate is answered and not which rows answer it.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE lines > 150 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 3

cases.name: a_negative_predicate_on_an_absent_column_drops_those_rows
cases.description: The arm that is easiest to get wrong, and the reason this is pinned against a real corpus rather than reasoned about. `!=` on a field a segment has no column for is FALSE for every row of that segment, not true: each arm of the row filter is `is_some_and`, so a missing value fails the operator rather than passing it. The corpus holds 59,636 rows and 3,903 of them answer `lines != 150` — the rest carry no `lines` at all and are dropped, before this change and after it. A reading that a negative predicate lets every row through would report tens of thousands here.

cases.name: a_negative_like_on_an_absent_column_drops_them_too
cases.description: `NOT LIKE` behaves as `!=` does and for the same reason, so the two are pinned together: 3,799 rows carry a `lines` value that does not start with 15. `NOT MATCHES` is the same rule again and is now pinned with them, in absent_value_fails_a_negation.json -- it did keep a row whose value resolved to nothing where a per-row evaluation dropped it, and holding every regex back to the built rows is what kept that disagreement off the answer; the two filters agree now, and the regex still waits for the compile alone.
cases.fql: FIND symbols WHERE lines NOT LIKE '15%' LIMIT 3
